content: 1. A feasibility study was conducted with secondary school students in Uganda to assess the acceptability and practicality of male circumcision interventions. (PLOS ONE, 2017) 2. Montano et al. identified key beliefs that motivate adult males in Zimbabwe to undergo circumcision, providing evidence-based targets for behavior change messaging. (AIDS and Behavior, 2014) 3. Moyo et al. explored how men's attitudes in rural Mhondoro-Ngezi, Zimbabwe, act as barriers to the demand for voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC). (Global Public Health, 2015) 4. Mwanga et al. analyzed the policy environment surrounding male circumcision for HIV prevention in Tanzania, highlighting key findings from a situational analysis. (BMC Public Health, 2011) 5. Nakyanjo et al. examined the role of women in promoting male circumcision in Rakai, Uganda, emphasizing their influence on decision-making processes. (AIDS Care, 2018) 6. Nevin et al. investigated perceptions of HIV and safe male circumcision in high HIV-prevalence fishing communities around Lake Victoria, Uganda. (PLOS ONE, 2015) 7. Osaki et al. studied the role of women in encouraging the uptake of VMMC in Tanzania, with a focus on their influence on male decision-making. (PLOS ONE, 2015) 8. Peltzer et al. reported on the prevalence and acceptability of male circumcision in South Africa, providing insights into cultural and social factors. (African Journal of Traditional, Complementary, and Alternative Medicines, 2014) 9. Plotkin et al. explored the social and individual factors affecting adult attendance at VMMC services in Tanzania, identifying barriers and motivators. (Global Health, Science and Practice, 2013) 10. Price et al. conducted narrative interviews with circumcision clients in Zambia to understand behavior change pathways leading to VMMC uptake. (PLOS ONE, 2014) 11. Rennie et al. examined perceptions of VMMC among circumcising and non-circumcising communities in Malawi, highlighting cultural and social dynamics. (Global Public Health, 2015) 12. Rupfutse et al. identified factors associated with the uptake of VMMC in Mazowe District, Zimbabwe, during 2014. (Pan African Medical Journal, 2014) 13. Sahay et al. conducted a multi-centric qualitative study in India to understand community and healthcare providers' perspectives on male circumcision. (PLOS ONE, 2014) 14. Shacham et al. explored perceptions of male circumcision among married couples in rural Malawi, focusing on its acceptability and implications for sexual health. (Journal of the International Association of Providers of AIDS Care, 2014) 15. Siegler et al. assessed the acceptability of medical male circumcision and improved instrument sanitation among traditionally circumcising groups in East Africa. (AIDS Behavior, 2012) 16. Skolnik et al. described motivations and barriers to VMMC in Lesotho through a cross-sectional study, providing insights into community attitudes. (BMC Public Health, 2014) 17. Ssekubugu et al. investigated contextual barriers and motivators to adult male medical circumcision in Rakai, Uganda, through qualitative research. (Qualitative Health Research, 2013) 18. Sullivan et al. studied attitudes toward circumcision among Chinese men, providing insights into cultural and social acceptability. (Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes, 2009) 19. Tapera et al. examined factors influencing the uptake of VMMC among male university students in Botswana, focusing on educational and social determinants. (International Journal of Health Promotion and Education, 2017) 20. Tieu et al. assessed the acceptability of male circumcision for HIV prevention among high-risk heterosexual men in Thailand. (Sexually Transmitted Diseases, 2010) 21. Tynan et al. explored community expectations and tensions in developing a male circumcision program for HIV prevention in Papua New Guinea. (BMC Public Health, 2013) 22. Walcott et al. identified factors associated with the acceptability of male circumcision among men in Jamaica, emphasizing cultural and social influences. (PLOS ONE, 2013) 23. Wang et al. studied the acceptability of VMMC among male patients with sexually transmitted diseases in China, focusing on their willingness to undergo the procedure. (PLOS ONE, 2016) 24. Westerkamp et al. examined circumcision preferences among women and uncircumcised men in Kenya prior to the scale-up of VMMC for HIV prevention. (AIDS Care, 2012) 25. Wilcken et al. conducted a cross-sectional study on awareness of male circumcision for HIV prevention among young people and adults in rural Uganda. (BMC Public Health, 2010) 26. Wirth et al. explored the decision-making process for undergoing medical male circumcision among adult men in Botswana through qualitative research. (AIDS Care, 2016) 27. Yang et al. investigated factors influencing Chinese men's willingness to undergo circumcision in western China, identifying cultural and social determinants. (PLOS ONE, 2012) 28. Zulu et al. studied sexual satisfaction, performance, and partner response following VMMC in Zambia as part of the Spear and Shield Project. (Global Health, Science and Practice, 2015) 29. Alfonso et al. analyzed trends in the marginal cost of male circumcision in rural Rakai, Uganda, providing insights into cost-effectiveness. (Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes, 2016) 30. Auvert et al. estimated the resources needed and savings anticipated from the roll-out of adult male circumcision in sub-Saharan Africa. (PLOS ONE, 2008) 31. Bautista-Arredondo et al. examined the influence of supply-side factors on VMMC costs in Kenya, Rwanda, South Africa, and Zambia. (PLOS ONE, 2018) 32. Binagwaho et al. conducted a cost-effectiveness study on male circumcision at different ages in Rwanda. (PLOS Medicine, 2010) 33. Bollinger et al. analyzed the cost and impact of male circumcision on HIV/AIDS in Botswana, providing evidence for policy decisions. (Journal of the International AIDS Society, 2009) 34. Debas et al. edited a comprehensive volume on essential surgery, including male circumcision, as part of disease control priorities. (World Bank, 2015) 35. Galárraga et al. conducted a systematic review of the cost-effectiveness of HIV prevention strategies, including male circumcision. (BMC Public Health, 2009) 36. George et al. evaluated the cost of demand creation activities targeting school-going adolescents for VMMC in South Africa. (PLOS ONE, 2017) 37. Kaufman et al. reported on a sport-based intervention to increase VMMC uptake among adolescent male students in Zimbabwe. (Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes, 2016) 38. Kripke et al. modeled the impact and cost-effectiveness of increased efforts to attract VMMC clients aged 20–29 in Zimbabwe. (PLOS ONE, 2016) 39. Kuznik et al. compared the cost of disposable versus reusable circumcision kits for HIV prevention in Uganda. (Tropical Doctor, 2012) 40. Larson et al. analyzed the cost of improving access to VMMC among high-risk, low-income communities in Uganda. (PLOS ONE, 2015) 41. Marseille et al. evaluated the cost and efficiency of alternative service delivery modes for adult male circumcision in Kenya. (BMC Health Services Research, 2014) 42. McGillen et al. assessed the emerging health impact of VMMC in Zimbabwe using three epidemiological models. (PLOS ONE, 2018) 43. Tchuenche et al. estimated client out-of-pocket costs for accessing VMMC in South Africa, providing insights into financial barriers. (PLOS ONE, 2016) 44. Tumwesigye et al. modeled the potential impact and cost of scaling up male circumcision in resource-poor settings in Uganda. (African Journal of AIDS Research, 2013) 45. Uthman et al. conducted a systematic review of economic evaluations of adult male circumcision for HIV prevention in sub-Saharan Africa. (PLOS ONE, 2010) 46. White et al. explored the timing, target populations, and strategies for male circumcision for HIV prevention in sub-Saharan Africa. (AIDS, 2008) 47. WHO and UNAIDS published a report on models to inform fast-tracking VMMC in HIV combination prevention. (World Health Organization, 2017) 48. Dionne et al. examined the influence of ethnic identity and region on attitudes toward male circumcision in a high HIV-prevalence country. (Global Public Health, 2013) 49. Hoffman et al. studied perceptions and knowledge of VMMC for HIV prevention in traditionally non-circumcising communities in South Africa. (Global Public Health, 2015) 50. Huang et al. identified factors associated with the acceptability of circumcision among male drug users in western China. (International Journal of STD & AIDS, 2013) 51. Brito et al. assessed the feasibility and acceptability of male circumcision among men, women, and healthcare providers in the Dominican Republic. (AIDS Care, 2010) 52. Carrasco et al. conducted a systematic review of barriers and facilitators to VMMC uptake in priority countries, providing recommendations for future strategies. (Sexually Transmitted Diseases, 2016) 53. Golub et al. examined the relationship between distance and post-operative visit attendance following VMMC in Kenya. (AIDS and Behavior, 2016) 54. Miiro et al. evaluated a soccer-based promotion of VMMC among secondary students in Uganda, using a mixed-methods feasibility study.
